prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I do kind gestures. Remove my appendix. I put my ear to a flat shell and—nothing. I play the lottery ironically. Get married. Have a smear test. I put my ear to the beak of a dead bird—nothing. I grow wisdom teeth. Jog. I pick up a toddler’s telephone, Hello?—No answer. I change a light bulb on my own. Organize a large party. Hire a clown. Attend a four-day stonewalling course. Have a baby. Stop eating Coco Pops. I put my ear right up to the slack and gaping bonnet of a daffodil—. Get divorced. Floss. Describe a younger person’s music taste as “just noise.” Enjoy perusing a garden center. Sit in a pub without drinking. I stand at the lip of a pouting valley—speak to me! My echo plagiarizes. I land a real love plus two real cats. I never meet the talking bird again. Or the yawning hole. The panther of purple wisps who prowls inside the air. I change nappies. Donate my eggs. Learn a profound lesson about sacrifice. Brunch. No singing floorboards. No vents leaking scentless instructions. My mission is over. The world has zipped up her second mouth.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker moves through adulthood via ordinary milestones such as marriage, parenthood, divorce, health procedures, and changing habits.
- Throughout these experiences, the speaker repeatedly searches for hidden voices or magical messages in nature and everyday objects but hears nothing.
- The speaker gradually adopts conventional adult behaviors, responsibilities, and tastes while reflecting humorously on aging.
- Love, family, sacrifice, and domestic life ultimately provide the speaker with meaningful forms of fulfillment.
- By the end, the speaker accepts that the mysterious, enchanted world has fallen silent and that the search is over.

The speaker traces adulthood through mundane milestones, relationships, parenthood, and repeated attempts to hear secret voices in shells, birds, flowers, valleys, and everyday objects. Finding only silence and imitation, they conclude that maturity has sealed off the world’s “second mouth,” signifying the loss of childhood wonder and enchantment.

outputs.L2: I perform small acts of kindness. My appendix is taken out. I press a flattened shell against my ear and hear nothing. As a joke, I buy lottery tickets. I marry. I undergo a cervical smear. I listen at the beak of a lifeless bird: silence again. My wisdom teeth come through. I take up jogging. I answer a toddler’s toy phone—Hello? Nobody replies. Without help, I replace a bulb. I arrange an enormous celebration and book a clown. I complete a four-day course in giving people the silent treatment. I give birth. Coco Pops disappear from my diet. outputs.L3:
The speaker moves through adulthood by way of familiar milestones: marriage, parenthood, divorce, medical procedures, and the gradual transformation of everyday habits. At each stage, the speaker continues to look for signs of mystery—for hidden voices in nature, magical messages in ordinary objects, or some indication that the world contains an enchanted meaning beyond daily experience. Yet no answer arrives. The natural and domestic worlds remain stubbornly silent.

As the years pass, the speaker increasingly takes on conventional adult responsibilities, preferences, and routines. Domestic obligations replace youthful wonder, while changing tastes and concerns reveal the effects of age. These changes are treated with humor and self-awareness, allowing the speaker to acknowledge the awkwardness and absurdity of growing older without becoming entirely bitter.

Although the long search for magic proves unsuccessful, adulthood is not presented as empty. Love, family, sacrifice, and domestic life offer quieter but more substantial forms of fulfillment. Marriage and parenthood bring difficulty and loss as well as tenderness, but they also give the speaker a sense of purpose that supernatural messages never provide.

By the end, the speaker accepts that the mysterious, enchanted world once hoped for has fallen silent. The search for hidden voices is finally abandoned. In its place is a mature recognition that meaning does not necessarily come through magic or revelation; it can be found in ordinary human attachments, responsibilities, and acts of love.
outputs.L4:
I became an adult by degrees, through events so ordinary that no one thought to mark them. I learned to sign my name at the bottom of forms, to wake before the alarm, to keep receipts in a drawer. I rented rooms with unreliable heat, bought groceries with careful arithmetic, and discovered how quickly a week could vanish into errands. Later came love, shared keys, arguments about money and dishes, reconciliations whispered after midnight. Then came children, with their sudden fevers and impossible questions, their small hands reaching for mine as if I knew the way.

All the while, I kept testing the world for hidden speech.

At the shore, I lifted shells to my ear, remembering the promise that an ocean lived inside them. I heard only the dull circulation of my own blood, a wind made by the body and mistaken for distance. In the garden, I bent close to flowers, expecting some delicate confidence to rise from their bright throats. There was fragrance, pollen, the faint scrape of an insect—but no message meant for me.

I listened to birds at dawn. Their calls seemed almost articulate, full of warning, gossip, and praise. I tried to separate their language from mere repetition, but every phrase dissolved into instinct and echo. In the hills, I called into valleys and waited. My own voice returned altered but not transformed. Even the echo had nothing new to say.

Years passed. The children grew. Their questions became practical, then private. The house filled with objects that once would have seemed enchanted: clocks, mirrors, locked cupboards, lamps glowing in empty rooms. I held each one to the old test. I pressed my ear to walls, pipes, radiators, closed doors. I listened to kettles beginning to boil, to floorboards settling at night, to rain speaking rapidly against the windows. Everywhere there was sound, but nowhere a secret voice.

Perhaps, when I was young, the world had two mouths. One named things plainly: stone, bird, flower, river. The other opened behind the first and spoke in riddles. A shell contained the sea; a tree remembered everyone who had touched it; darkness was a country, and every path might lead beyond the visible edge of things. Nothing was merely itself.

Adulthood taught me otherwise. It taught me causes, mechanisms, and reasonable explanations. It showed me how echoes work, why pipes knock, why birds sing, why shells seem to murmur. Each answer was useful. Each answer closed a door.

Now, when I place a shell against my ear, I know what I am hearing. When a bird repeats its call, I recognize the pattern. When the valley throws back my words, I do not mistake them for a reply. The world still has its first mouth: the one that announces weather, hunger, birth, work, love, illness, and death. It speaks constantly, and I have learned to understand it.

But the second mouth is sealed.

Whether it belonged to the world or only to the child I was, I cannot say. I know only that once I expected everything to answer, and now I expect nothing. The silence is not emptiness; it is knowledge. Yet sometimes, holding an ordinary object in the evening light, I wait a moment longer than reason requires, hoping the hidden mouth will open again.
outputs.L5: To create space for new opportunities, we sometimes need to **remove** what no longer serves us. When we let go of unnecessary habits, objects, or worries, we can **get** a clearer view of what truly matters. In the end, it is not about how much we **have**, but how wisely we use and appreciate it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about someone moving through adulthood while repeatedly trying—and failing—to hear secret messages from ordinary objects, ending with the realization that the world has fallen silent.
counterfactuals.output:
At twenty-three, she held a drinking glass to the wall and waited for the plaster to confess. The neighbors were arguing about money; pipes knocked in their sleep. Beneath it all, she was certain, the building knew her true name. But the glass gave her only the warm weather of her own breath.

At thirty, she pressed an ear to the office photocopier. Each page emerged pale and feverish, bearing charts no one believed and numbers that climbed ladders into fog. She thought the machine might whisper, *Leave before your hands become paper.* Instead it hummed with the patience of a refrigerator in an empty house.

Marriage arrived wearing shoes full of rain. She listened to the wedding rings by placing them on the kitchen table at midnight. They said nothing. She listened to the kettle, the mortgage, the blue toothbrush leaning toward the red one like a flower seeking light. Silence hid inside every object, small and hard as a seed.

When her mother died, she lifted the dead woman’s sewing box and shook it gently. Buttons clicked like distant planets. Needles flashed their silver grammar. Surely grief had translated everything; surely the thimble, which had known the pressure of that vanished finger, would speak. But it remained a little metal cup, brimming with no one.

Years passed through her body disguised as weather. She bent toward parking meters, elevator buttons, supermarket oranges. She asked the smoke alarm for prophecy, the cracked phone for forgiveness, the lamp for instructions on how to grow old. Even the coins in her pocket—those tiny moons rubbed smooth by strangers—refused to tell her where they had been.

At last, in a room emptied of all but a chair, she placed her ear against the floor. She waited for the buried city, the roots exchanging secrets, the earth turning its enormous key.

Nothing came.

Then she understood: the messages had not been hidden from her. They had not been delayed, or spoken in a language she had failed to learn. One by one, while she was busy becoming an adult, the objects had closed their mouths.

The world had fallen silent.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented first-person monologue that interweaves mundane milestones like marriage, divorce, parenthood, brunch, flossing, and changing light bulbs with eerie memories of a once-magical talking world.
counterfactuals.output:
I married in June because June was available.

The venue had folding chairs, a dry fountain, and a coordinator who kept saying *timeless* while checking her watch. I remember the vows. I remember the cake sweating in the heat.

I also remember the lilacs whispering, *Don’t do it.*

But flowers had always been dramatic.

—

Our daughter was born at 3:17 in the morning. Seven pounds, furious, perfect. The nurse placed her on my chest and she opened her eyes as if she recognized me from somewhere else.

“Hello,” I said.

Behind the hospital wall, something with many small feet said, *At last.*

No one else heard.

—

We used to live in a world where everything spoke.

Not metaphorically.

Teacups complained about the cold. Roads hummed beneath tires. The moon lowered itself between the trees and asked children riddles in a voice like a wet finger circling glass.

I think we were happier then.

Or we were terrified all the time and called it wonder.

—

On Sundays we went to brunch.

Eggs, coffee, a tiny iron cup of syrup. Our daughter colored on the paper menu while my husband—then my husband—read headlines on his phone.

The saltshaker leaned toward me.

*He has already left,* it said.

“Could you pass the salt?” I asked.

He did.

That was almost worse.

—

The divorce took eight months and three thousand signatures.

The mediator wore a blue cardigan. We divided the books, the dishes, the holidays, the debt. We spoke calmly about custody. We did not mention the door in the woods, or the year the crows learned our names, or the golden animal that slept beneath our kitchen and promised to keep the house standing as long as we loved each other.

After he moved out, the floor sagged.

Just a little.

—

I floss every night now.

This is how I know I’m doing better.

Waxed mint thread. Upper left, upper right. The hygienist says my gums have improved. Sometimes, when the floss slips between two molars, I taste the black river that ran behind my childhood home.

It used to call to us after dark.

Not by name.

By the things we would become.

Mother, it called me.

Wife.

Stranger.

—

My daughter says she doesn’t remember the talking world.

She remembers preschool, chicken nuggets, the apartment with the radiator that knocked. She remembers her father crying in the grocery store beside the birthday cards.

“But the wolves?” I ask.

“What wolves?”

“The ones who taught you to sing.”

She rolls her eyes. She is fourteen.

There are no wolves now. Only their pale tracks sometimes appearing in the steam on the bathroom mirror.

—

Yesterday, the hallway bulb burned out.

I fetched the stepladder, unscrewed the dead glass, and shook it beside my ear. Something inside rattled.

Not the filament.

A voice.

Very faint.

*You have forgotten the way back.*

I put in a new bulb. Warm white, sixty watts. The hallway filled with ordinary light.

For one second, every closed door breathed.

Then the refrigerator clicked on. My daughter called from her room to ask what was for dinner. My ex texted about next weekend. Outside, a delivery truck reversed with three patient beeps.

I carried the dead bulb to the trash.

It whispered all the way down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an absurdist list-poem charting a woman’s life from youthful wonder to conventional adulthood. Include dead birds, toy telephones, daffodils, an echo, cats, fertility, and the final image of the world “zipping up her second mouth.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Inventory of a Woman, Arranged by Age**

At five, she kept three dead birds  
in a shoebox labeled **SKY—SPARE PARTS**.

At seven, toy telephones rang beneath her bed.  
She answered each one:  
*Hello, this is the moon.*  
The moon always asked for her mother.

At nine, she believed daffodils  
were yellow trumpets rehearsing spring,  
and knelt to conduct them  
with a licorice wand.

At twelve, she shouted her name into a well.  
An echo returned it  
wearing lipstick.

At fifteen, cats gathered on the roof  
to vote on her future.  
The motion passed by whisker.

At eighteen, wonder was still a country,  
but the border guards had begun  
to inspect her luggage.

At twenty-two, she carried fertility  
like an unopened umbrella—  
useful, ominous,  
always taking up room in the hall.

At twenty-six, relatives served advice  
in porcelain cups:  
marry, save, moisturize,  
do not alarm the neighbors.

At thirty, she bought curtains,  
a calendar,  
six matching forks,  
and a small mechanical weather  
for the kitchen.

At thirty-four, the toy telephones rang again.  
This time she said,  
*I’m sorry, the moon no longer lives here.*

At thirty-eight, daffodils arrived  
in a supermarket sleeve,  
their trumpets full of receipts.

At forty, she dreamed of the dead birds  
opening their shoebox  
and flying the cardboard south.

At forty-five, the cats stopped voting.  
They had become management.

At fifty, her echo moved into the spare room,  
paid no rent,  
and answered every question correctly.

At sixty, she wore convention  
like a sensible coat  
with one impossible feather in the lining.

At seventy, she found wonder again  
under the sink,  
beside the bleach,  
still bright, still biting.

And at the end,  
after the forks, the forms, the flowers,  
after fertility had folded its umbrella,  
after the moon had forgotten her number,  
the world leaned close,  
took hold of the years,  
and began zipping up her second mouth.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a darkly comic piece of experimental flash fiction in which the narrator searches shells, flowers, valleys, vents, and floorboards for supernatural voices, but each adult rite of passage makes those voices harder to hear.
counterfactuals.output:
**TERMS AND CONDITIONS MAY APPLY**

At seven, I held a conch to my ear.

The dead were having a beach party inside.

They sang off-key. They complained about the sand. One voice—possibly my future self—kept shouting, *Don’t eat the shrimp.*

My mother said it was only the sea.

We lived three hundred miles from the sea.

At thirteen, I interrogated flowers.

Daffodils knew nothing. Roses demanded a lawyer. Foxgloves whispered precise instructions for poisoning a duke, though we had no duke and, after budget cuts, barely a mayor.

I wrote everything down.

Then puberty arrived with its paperwork. My bones lengthened. My face became a public argument. At my confirmation, the bishop pressed his thumb to my forehead and asked whether I renounced Satan.

“Which one?” I said.

The flowers went quiet for a year.

*

At eighteen, I drove into valleys and called down to the supernatural.

“HELLO?”

*Hello,* the valleys returned.

“IS ANYONE THERE?”

*Anyone there?*

“WHAT SHOULD I DO WITH MY LIFE?”

There was a long pause.

Then: *Retail.*

I enrolled in business school.

By graduation, the echoes had developed poor reception. They spoke only in fragments:

*—run—*

*—before—*

*—quarterly targets—*

My academic adviser called this “career readiness.”

*

In my first apartment, voices came through the heating vents.

They were faint but practical.

*Your neighbor is stealing your mail.*

*The landlord painted over a door.*

*There is something in the basement wearing your old teeth.*

I listened nightly, cheek against the grate, until I received my first promotion.

The company gave me a laminated badge with my photograph on it. In the photograph I looked pre-haunted.

After that, the vents mostly said:

*Optimize.*

*Circle back.*

*Per my previous scream.*

When I married, the officiant asked us to repeat our vows. Beneath the floorboards, something repeated them too, half a second late.

“In sickness and in health,” I said.

*In thickness and in wealth,* said the floor.

My spouse heard only mice.

We bought traps.

*

The mortgage closing took place in a windowless room. We signed our names forty-three times, each signature smaller than the last, until we had transferred our souls into a ranch-style home with structural concerns.

That first night, I pried up a floorboard.

Below it: dust, one marble, a child’s molar, and a darkness so old it had tenure.

“Speak,” I whispered.

The darkness cleared its throat.

The refrigerator began making ice.

*

Then came parenthood, that ancient rite in which adults voluntarily summon a person and spend years preventing it from returning to the spirit realm.

Our baby screamed at corners.

“What do you see?” I asked.

The baby stared over my shoulder, delighted.

“Is it Grandma?”

The baby laughed.

“Is it death?”

The baby laughed harder.

“Is death wearing Grandma?”

The baby fell asleep.

I put my ear to shells, petals, valleys, vents, floorboards. Everywhere, the voices had receded behind grocery lists, insurance premiums, school forms, passwords requiring one uppercase letter and one symbol of existential despair.

At my father’s funeral, I leaned over his coffin.

“Dad?”

Nothing.

I checked beneath the flowers.

Nothing.

I pressed my ear to the polished wood.

At last, a whisper:

*We’ve been trying to reach you about—*

The crematorium started up.

*

Now I am old enough to be addressed as “sir” by people carrying defibrillators.

I keep the conch on my desk.

Sometimes, at 3:17 a.m., when the house contracts around its nails and the vents exhale their warm institutional breath, I lift it to my ear.

The party is still going.

Far away, the dead are singing. Someone uncorks a bottle. Someone dives laughing into the black water.

I strain to hear what they are saying.

But my hearing aid needs charging.

And the shell, apparently, has accepted a management position.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine a character who once encountered talking birds, mysterious holes, and creatures made of purple mist. Tell the rest of her life as a breathless sequence of clipped sentences, mixing surreal loss with banal achievements and social expectations.
counterfactuals.output:
She came home before supper. Mud on her stockings. Feathers in her hair. Nobody asked the right questions.

She grew taller. Learned fractions. Forgot the birds’ true names. Won a handwriting prize. Lost the brass key. Smiled for photographs. Dreamed of the holes opening beneath the dining table, neat as buttonholes, breathing cold air.

At sixteen she was told to be sensible. At seventeen she became sensible. At eighteen she saw purple mist collecting in the school corridor. It wore her mother’s face. She walked through it. Passed her examinations.

There was a job. Then another job. A desk with three drawers. A supervisor who praised her punctuality. She married a man who disliked riddles. They bought curtains. They bought a kettle. They bought insurance against fire, theft, flood, never against vanishing.

Two children arrived. Loud. Pink. Astonishing. She taught them manners. Hid crumbs for birds on the sill. Checked beneath their beds for holes. Found only dust, a marble, one small tooth.

Years hurried. Promotions. Funerals. Dental appointments. The purple creatures returned whenever someone died. They waited politely beside the grave. Hatless. Shivering. She never introduced them.

Her husband grew tired. The children grew distant, then affectionate, then busy. She learned to drive. Burned a roast. Joined a committee. Resigned from the committee. Received a certificate for twenty-five years of service. Mislaid it behind the boiler.

At sixty she began hearing wings inside the walls. At seventy she answered them. People called this decline. People lowered their voices. People brought casseroles.

She remained courteous. Took her pills. Wrote thank-you notes. Watched the garden sink, inch by inch, into a darkness no surveyor could measure.

On her last morning she dressed carefully. Blue coat. Clean shoes. Pearl earrings. Social expectations observed.

Then the oldest bird landed on the windowsill.

Late, it said.

I know, she said.

The floor opened.

Purple mist rose like applause.

She stepped down without falling.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
